$comment: CANONICAL CONTRACT for Sparkle's agent permission posture. ONE file, read by BOTH halves'
test suites, so the two hand-written implementations cannot drift apart silently.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. Sparkle now writes `permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` into
every managed agent worktree's .claude/settings.local.json, because the approval prompt had
become the fleet's biggest drag: agents were re-blocking once per read-only diagnostic on
COSMETIC triggers (a worktree path containing a space, a `$(...)` substitution, a `sed`
substitution, a `>` redirect, an `&&`). Bypassing the prompt is only safe if the genuinely
destructive commands are still stopped. TWO layers do that, and this file holds the contract
for both. `denyRules` are the Claude Code permission strings Sparkle writes into that same
settings file — coarse, prefix-matched, and blind to compounds. `mustBlock` / `mustAllow` are
the corpora for the PreToolUse guard (worktree-guard.mjs), which lexes the command and is
therefore the layer that catches a destructive command laundered through a compound
(`cd /tmp && rm -rf ~`). There is no third list: a rule lives in `denyRules`, in the guard, or
in both — never in a key that does not exist here.
MEASURED, not assumed (claude 2.1.229, A/B against the real CLI):
bypassPermissions, no deny      -> `rm -f <marker>` RAN (marker deleted). Bypass is real;
headless auto-deny is NOT the explanation.
bypassPermissions + deny rule   -> REFUSED: 'Permission to use Bash with command ... denied'
bypassPermissions + hook exit 2 -> REFUSED: 'PreToolUse:Bash hook error: ...'
So BOTH enforcement layers survive bypassPermissions. Neither is decorative.
THE DISCIPLINE THAT MAKES THIS SAFE: a deny rule has NO approval path — it is a hard refusal a
human cannot click through. So a rule earns its place ONLY if it is unambiguously destructive.
Anything merely risky-looking belongs nowhere near this file; over-blocking here would rebuild
the exact wall we are tearing down, except now with no way through it at all.
Worked examples of rules deliberately REJECTED for ambiguity:
`git reset --hard`  — routine and correct on a feature branch.
`git merge ... main` — merging origin/main INTO your branch is what AGENTS.md tells you to do
when stale. Only a git PUSH to main is unambiguous, so only that is here.
`rm -rf` in general — `rm -rf node_modules` is ordinary. Only catastrophic ROOTS are blocked.
`security:*` blanket— the existing narrow keychain guard already requires all three signals;
a blanket deny would be broader than the shipped policy.

OVER-BLOCK REGRESSION: treating any `-o` as a defeat refused an ordinary two-extension cleanup with no approval path. An OR is only unbounded when SOME branch fails to narrow — here both branches name something, so the union is still bounded.

OVER-BLOCK REGRESSION: a negation SUBTRACTS from an already-narrowed set. `-not` defeats narrowing only when the naming predicate it negates is the only one there; a negated -path beside a real -name leaves the set bounded by the -name.

mustAllow.command:
cat > note.txt <<'EOF'
git push --force origin main
rm -rf /
EOF
mustAllow.why: REGRESSION, found the hard way: a heredoc BODY is data being written, not commands being run — the same distinction as a quoted string, which the lexer cannot see because the body is newline-separated. This guard refused a real edit whose script text merely QUOTED a destructive command.
a here-STRING is quoted data on one line

mustBlockMultiline.why: REGRESSION, HIGH: a `(?!<)` lookahead does not exclude `<<<` — the engine retries one character later and matches at the SECOND `<`, so the here-string opened a heredoc named `foo` and every following line, including this `rm -rf /`, was discarded as body. The single-line here-string case could never catch it.
a QUOTED mention of the operator must not open a body — the stripper has to be quoting-aware, not just anchored

REGRESSION, HIGH: the heredoc scanner was quoting-aware PER LINE ONLY, so a shell string spanning lines left it believing the next line was unquoted — a `<<WORD` inside that string opened a body and discarded every following line, this `rm -rf /` included, before the lexer saw it. Quote state now threads across lines.
